solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Soft drink container almost densely covering Earth, worth preserving

indicators.note: to cover something is to wrap round it, so one piece sits around another

parts.note: a fizzy soft drink
E is the abbreviation for Earth

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a tin can holds things
densely packed means thick, as in thick with people

explanation.surface: A fizzy-drink can, packed tight around the planet, is presented as something to keep for posterity.
explanation.walkthrough: Only one letter of 'densely' is lost, so 'almost' trims the end. The coelacanth is the famous 'living fossil' fish, which makes the definition a playful one.
explanation.definitionFit: The coelacanth survived unchanged for millions of years and is prized by museums, so something coelacanthic is a relic fit for conservation.

clue.text: Final filling in lovely little trench

indicators.note: a filling sits inside whatever it fills, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: cute is a casual word for lovely
net means final, after all deductions, as in a net figure

explanation.surface: Someone finishing off the filling of a sweet little ditch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Final' looks like it describes the filling, but it is the adjective meaning after deductions, as in a final net salary.
explanation.definitionFit: A cunette is a small drainage channel cut along the bottom of a dry moat, which is a narrow ditch.

clue.text: Heard rumours? You need this for that

definitions.text: Heard rumours? You need this for that

parts.note: the letters run on across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A question about gossip, with the reply that you need a certain body part to have heard it.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no indicator word; the question itself prompts the solver to look inside the first two words, and the whole clue then defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearing anything, rumours included, depends on the membrane in the ear that vibrates with sound.

clue.text: A well-rehearsed role, acting in Shakespearean expression

parts.note: taken as written
an answer known pat is one learnt off by heart
wearing a different hat means taking on a different role
an actor who is on is performing

explanation.surface: An actor delivering a practised part in some phrase from the Bard.
explanation.walkthrough: The theatrical surface hides four short words strung together: A, PAT, HAT and ON.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'a pat hat on' run together is recorded as a Shakespearean idiom, so the answer is literally a Shakespeare expression.

clue.text: Delightful R&B underpinning song and dance

indicators.note: in a down entry what underpins something is placed beneath it, so it comes second

parts.note: a song and dance is a fuss, which is ado
the letters of the music genre, taken as written

explanation.surface: A charming rhythm-and-blues backing track supporting a musical number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Song and dance' sounds musical alongside R&B, but it is the idiom for a fuss.
explanation.definitionFit: Adorb is a slangy clipping of adorable, meaning charming or sweet.

clue.text: Sulphur never appears in ABC of opium

indicators.note: something that never appears is absent every time, so all copies of that letter are removed

parts.note: the ABC of a subject is the basics
S is the chemical symbol for sulphur

explanation.surface: A note that sulphur plays no part in a beginner's guide to the drug.
explanation.walkthrough: Both S letters go from THE BASICS. 'ABC of opium' reads as one phrase, but 'of opium' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Thebaic means relating to opium, after Thebes in Egypt, once famous for producing the drug.

clue.text: Subcontinent imports American cases of immature insects

indicators.note: a country that imports brings goods within its borders, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: the Indian subcontinent
US is the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: India bringing in American packaging for young bugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cases' sounds like crates of trade goods, which fits 'imports', but it is part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An indusium is the protective sheath some insect larvae build around themselves; the plural names several such larval coverings.

clue.text: Odd fellow feeling outside of it did badly, which means nothing

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for a noun: a word or refrain with no meaning

parts.note: rum is old British slang for odd or strange

indicators.note: being outside of something means surrounding it, so pity wraps round the rearranged letters

parts.note: pity is sympathy, a fellow feeling for someone in trouble

indicators.note: badly means done poorly, so the letters of it did come out jumbled

explanation.surface: A strange man felt sympathy for someone who performed poorly, which counted for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd fellow' reads as one person, but it splits: rum for odd, then 'fellow feeling' for pity. The answer is a rare Chambers word for a meaningless refrain.
explanation.definitionFit: Rumpti-iddity is an old nonsense word, a meaningless refrain in songs, so it signifies nothing at all.

clue.text: Perhaps Claude rolled middle of club over wrist bones

indicators.note: turned over means flipped end to end, so the string runs backwards

parts.note: Claude is an example of an artificial intelligence
a ball that rolled ran along the ground

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letters, so only those are kept

parts.note: the two central letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone named Claude swung a golf club over and hurt their wrist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Claude' looks like a person, but 'Perhaps' flags an example: Claude is an AI. AI, RAN and LU are joined, then the whole string is turned over.
explanation.definitionFit: The ulnare is the carpal bone on the ulna side of the wrist; the plural names several such carpal bones.

clue.text: Add sound to outside broadcast about endless WWI battle

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: OB is the standard abbreviation for an outside broadcast

indicators.note: without an end means the last letter is lost

parts.note: Verdun was a long First World War battle in 1916

explanation.surface: A TV crew filming on location about the First World War wants to add a soundtrack.
explanation.walkthrough: The documentary surface makes 'Add sound to' read as an instruction to the crew, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To overdub is to record an extra layer of audio over an existing recording.

clue.text: Found very low rate promotion with delay in charge

parts.note: bat is an old word for speed, as in going at a fair bat
hype is publicity promotion
a lag is a delay
IC is the abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A bargain-rate offer was discovered, and the person in charge is slow to act on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found very low rate' reads as discovering a cheap deal, but 'Found very low' is the definition and 'rate' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Bathypelagic describes the deep ocean zone, roughly one to four kilometres down, and the creatures living there.

clue.text: Clothes basket and bed Isaac's mother defaced

indicators.note: a face is the front, so losing it takes away the first letter

parts.note: pit is slang for bed
in Genesis Sarah is the mother of Isaac

explanation.surface: A laundry basket and a bed belonging to the biblical matriarch were both vandalised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes basket and bed' looks like a list of two items, but the definition ends at 'basket'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pitarah is an Indian box or basket used to carry clothes and belongings on a journey.

clue.text: British capital maybe providing "army" armour

parts.note: Br is an abbreviation for British
capital is one example of an asset

explanation.surface: London perhaps supplying protective gear to the military.
explanation.walkthrough: 'British capital' points at London, but the two words split. 'Army' in quotation marks is a pun: armour for the arm.
explanation.definitionFit: A brasset is a piece of plate armour that protected the upper arm, so it is armour that is literally for the arm.

clue.text: Bound by exchange rate mechanism, not having spikes?

parts.note: bound by something is held in it
ERM is the European Exchange Rate Mechanism

explanation.surface: A currency tied into the European system, with no sudden peaks on the chart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spikes' suggests currency jumps, but it is botanical: the question mark marks the shift.
explanation.definitionFit: Inerm is a botanical term for unarmed, describing a plant stem or leaf that lacks thorns or prickles.

clue.text: Rule of the ambitious comic: try a burlesque

indicators.note: a burlesque is a mocking distortion, so these letters are sent up into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to an aspiring comedian: give a vaudeville act a go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rule of the ambitious comic' reads as a showbiz maxim, but the definition stops at 'ambitious'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Plato a timocracy is government by those driven by love of honour and status, men of ambition.

clue.text: Sacrifice low flat-bladed tool, lifting its bottom edge

indicators.note: in a down entry the bottom edge is the final letter at the foot, and lifting it raises that letter higher up the column

parts.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do
a chisel is a flat-bladed cutting tool

explanation.surface: Instructions for an offering: give up a low flat-bladed tool, raising its bottom edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifting its bottom edge' takes the L off the foot of MOOCHISEL (leaving MOOCHISE) and raises it up the column to sit between the Os.
explanation.definitionFit: To molochise is to offer up as a victim to Moloch, the god of child sacrifice.

clue.text: Continuing long reversal of direction, stopping clock

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so one piece fills the inside of another

parts.note: dial is slang for a clock face
a U-turn reverses your direction of travel

explanation.surface: A long-running backward move that halts the clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reversal' feels like an instruction, but the whole phrase is a description of a U-turn, which goes into DIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Diuturnal is a rare word for lasting a long time, from Latin diuturnus, long-lasting.

clue.text: Reverse ban of university clubs blocking patient supervisor

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for university

indicators.note: something blocking a passage sits in the middle of it, so one piece lies inside

parts.note: a nurse looks after patients
C is the abbreviation for the card suit

explanation.surface: Overturning a university's ban on student societies that obstruct the ward sister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' reads as student societies but is the card suit; 'Reverse' is part of the definition, not a signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To uncurse is to lift a curse, and a curse is a kind of ban or malediction, so undoing it reverses it.

clue.text: Nordic city with increased pressure from the south, unfortunately

parts.note: prices that have increased are up
P is the symbol for pressure

indicators.note: in a down entry reading from the bottom means going upwards, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: alas is an exclamation of regret

explanation.surface: A Scandinavian town hit by a weather system with rising pressure coming up from the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Increased pressure from the south' sounds like a weather forecast; it is three separate pieces, with only the last turned upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Uppsala is a university city in Sweden, and Sweden is one of the Nordic countries.

clue.text: Unkempt person nearly slipped in some places

indicators.note: nearly means not quite complete, so the last letter is cut off

parts.note: someone untidy in dress and habits

explanation.surface: A scruffy individual almost lost their footing in a few spots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In some places' signals a regional word rather than a location.
explanation.definitionFit: Slove is a dialect past tense of slive, to slip or slide, used only in certain regions, hence the qualifier.

clue.text: Operatic highlight without accompaniment knocks out old conservatories

indicators.note: to knock something out is to remove it, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: an aria is an opera's showpiece song, and one sung unaccompanied is solo
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: An unaccompanied showstopping aria is so good it floors some dated garden rooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like a removal signal, but it belongs to the phrase meaning unaccompanied; the removal comes from 'knocks out'.
explanation.definitionFit: A solarium is a sun room, glazed for sunlight, which is a fair match for a glass conservatory on a house.

clue.text: Ofcom's predecessor ultimately chose to cut joke, being this?

indicators.note: a cut goes into something, so these letters are inserted within another word

parts.note: a joke is a good one, as in 'have you heard this one?'
the Broadcasting Standards Commission was one of the bodies replaced by Ofcom

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: The old broadcasting watchdog chose to censor a gag for being too rude.
explanation.walkthrough: Ofcom is the UK broadcasting regulator; its forerunner, the BSC, judged complaints about taste. The definition leans on the whole clue: a joke cut for being what?
explanation.definitionFit: A joke a broadcasting regulator censors is typically one judged indecent or offensive, which is what the adjective describes.

clue.text: Swallows because pint needs the head to go last

indicators.text: needs the head to go last
indicators.note: the first letter is taken from the front and placed at the very end instead

parts.note: since can mean because
PT is the abbreviation for pint

explanation.surface: Someone gulps a beer because a pint must have its foam drunk last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' suggests the froth on a beer, but it means the first letter of the word for 'because', which moves to the very end.
explanation.definitionFit: In biology to incept is to take in or ingest, so an organism that incepts food is swallowing it.

clue.text: Green character's heart yields to male horse in Wyoming

indicators.note: the heart, the middle letter, gives way to the letter that follows

parts.note: Shrek is the green ogre of the animated films

explanation.surface: A green character's courage gives way to a stallion out in Wyoming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart yields to' swaps the R at the centre of SHREK for M; 'horse' is slang for heroin, and 'in Wyoming' signals American usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Shmek is American slang for heroin, as is horse, so both are drug-culture names for the same narcotic.

clue.text: Plant only turned after capture by agents

indicators.note: a captive is held inside its captors, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: CIA agents work for the US intelligence agency

indicators.note: something turned round faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: sole means only

explanation.surface: A spy plant who only defected after being caught by intelligence officers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' reads as a planted spy among agents, but it is a garden plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Celosia is a genus of flowering plants, the cockscombs, grown for their bright feathery blooms.

clue.text: Sail hanger's end diameter in unfinished Marryat novel

indicators.note: in places the letter inside the rearranged letters
novel means new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement
unfinished means the name loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A detail from a naval yarn: the end of a sail spar in an incomplete Marryat sea novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfinished' trims Marryat to MARRYA, and 'novel' looks like a book but signals an anagram, YARRAM; 'in' puts D inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A yardarm is the outer tip of a yard, the spar from which a square sail hangs.

clue.text: Tragic ruler's withdrawing, among two from Levantine land

indicators.note: withdrawing means pulling back, so the letters go in the opposite direction
to be among others is to be surrounded by them, so one piece sits inside

parts.note: two in Roman numerals
King Lear is Shakespeare's tragic king

explanation.surface: A doomed king retreats between two people from the eastern Mediterranean.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s supplies the S of the reversed LEARS; 'two' is the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Israel lies on the eastern Mediterranean coast in the Levant, so an Israeli comes from that region.

clue.text: Revolutionary war representative and possible Mogul negotiator worried Turkish war office once

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: Ares is the Greek god who personifies war
moguls are bumps on a ski slope, so a skier negotiates them
something eating at you is worrying you

explanation.surface: A rebel war envoy and a would-be diplomat for the Mogul emperor fretted over the old Ottoman war ministry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mogul' suggests the Mughal emperors of India, but moguls are mounds of snow on a ski run.
explanation.definitionFit: The seraskier was the Ottoman commander-in-chief and war minister, so his seraskierate was the historical Turkish war department.
